abstract_2: This project proposes GV-YOLO26, a lightweight real-time detector for speed bumps and potholes built on YOLO26n, the newest end-to-end member of the YOLO family. We redesigned its backbone and neck around cheap convolutions: GhostConv layers replace the costly downsampling convolutions of the deeper stages, and VoVGSCSPC blocks built from GSConv replace the C3k2 feature blocks. A high-resolution P2 detection level is added for small, distant targets, and a Lightweight Grouped Detection Head (LGDH) with shared grouped convolutions keeps the extra level affordable while retaining the NMS-free one-to-one prediction of YOLO26. In its final form GV-YOLO26 has 1.57 million parameters and needs 5.1 GFLOPs, 34% fewer parameters and less computation than YOLO26n (2.38 million, 5.3 GFLOPs), even though it predicts on an extra 160 × 160 grid. Training incorporates a Normalized Wasserstein Distance (NWD) box loss and weather augmentation; knowledge distillation from a larger GV-YOLO26 teacher was also evaluated, and an in-video hazard detection pipeline with temporal tracking was demonstrated, with embedded hardware acceleration identified as future work.
abstract_3: To choose the base model on evidence, we first benchmarked seven stock detectors, from YOLOv8n to YOLO26n and RT-DETR-L, on the SBP-YOLO road hazard dataset; YOLO26n was the most accurate at 74.8% mAP@0.5 and the cheapest at 5.3 GFLOPs. GV-YOLO26 was then trained stage by stage through an ablation ladder on the 7,600-image SBP-YOLO dataset. We found that 47% of the dataset's raw test images are augmented copies or video frames of training scenes, and evaluated every model on a leakage-free held-out set of 482 images instead. There GV-YOLO26 reached 77.5% mAP@0.5 against 81.0% for an identically trained YOLO26n baseline, with 34% fewer parameters, running at 57.5 FPS in PyTorch FP32 on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU. Distillation did not improve accuracy: as implemented, its box term was unbounded and destabilised training. An in-video demo links detections across frames with ByteTrack and warns only about hazards confirmed over three frames. TensorRT edge acceleration and embedded Jetson deployment are formulated as future work.
dataset_para: The SBP-YOLO dataset (speed12) comprises 7,600 images across train/, valid/, and test/ folders. Before evaluation, the dataset required rigorous verification. File names and image hashes show that many images in test/ and valid/ are augmented copies of photos in train/: for example, train/ holds add_gasuss_noise_1386_jpg.rf.df5cd630….jpg, a noise-augmented copy of the test image 1386_jpg.rf.df5cd630….jpg with an identical visual hash. Other files represent neighbouring frames from sequential dashcam or GoPro video drives. We traced every image back to its source photo and drive. Of the 1,125 test images, 526 share a source photo with train/ and 839 share a photo or video sequence; of the 750 valid images, 554 do. Scores on the raw test split therefore reward memorisation as well as detection. To ensure strict academic integrity, all main experimental results in Chapter 5 are reported on the remaining 482 images (286 from test/ and 196 from valid/), which share zero source photos, videos, or drives with the training partition. This leakage-free held-out set contains 354 pothole instances in 145 images and 384 speed bump instances in 337 images. Each pothole in a cluster is annotated individually, and speed bump bounding boxes cover the full road width, conventions that make strict-IoU metrics lower for potholes than for speed bumps.

ch4_summary: This chapter described the design and implementation of GV-YOLO26. The network rebuilds the YOLO26n backbone and neck with GhostConv and VoVGSCSPC, adds a P2 detection level for small targets, and offsets its cost with the LGDH while keeping NMS-free inference; the training recipe adds the NWD loss and weather augmentation, and distillation was tested. For video, ByteTrack links detections across frames and a temporal confirmation rule suppresses one-frame false alarms. Seven stock detectors trained on the SBP-YOLO dataset justify the choice of YOLO26n as the base, and every design stage is evaluated on a leakage-free held-out set. The next chapter presents the results.
ch5_intro: This chapter presents the experimental results of the project. It begins with the benchmark of seven stock detectors on the SBP-YOLO dataset that was used to select the base model, then reports the 6-stage ablation study of GV-YOLO26, the distillation experiments, computational efficiency and PyTorch inference latency profiling, and the in-video demo, and finally compares the proposed model with earlier published work. Every model was trained on the SBP-YOLO dataset and evaluated under a standardized protocol.
setup_baselines: We trained seven stock detectors on the training partition of the SBP-YOLO dataset with the configuration in Table 4.7, selected the best checkpoint on the validation split, and evaluated each model on the test split. Latency was measured on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU as the end-to-end time of a single-image prediction, averaged over 100 test images.
setup_gv: Each design stage in Table 4.5 was trained with the configuration in Table 4.6 on the 5,243 training images of the SBP-YOLO dataset; its best checkpoint was selected on the 586-image validation split, and it was evaluated once on the leakage-free held-out set (482 images) and on the raw 1,125-image test split. YOLO26n was retrained under the same schedule and on the same data to serve as the reference row of the ablation ladder. Latency and computational cost were measured with tools/benchmark.py in PyTorch FP32 on a Tesla T4 GPU.
setup_latency: Computational complexity and inference throughput were evaluated in PyTorch FP32 on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU at batch size 1, measuring end-to-end latency per image over 100 test images after 10 warm-up images. Model parameter counts, GFLOPs, and .pt checkpoint file sizes were recorded. Dedicated TensorRT conversion and embedded edge deployment are formulated as future work in Chapter 6. The in-video demo was run with demo_video.py on four 10-second dashcam-style clips at 1280 × 720 and 24 frames per second, on the CPU of a laptop (Intel Core i5-1240P), the most constrained hardware in the project.
baseline_para: Table 5.1 and Fig. 5.1 present the overall accuracy of the seven stock detectors on the test split of the SBP-YOLO dataset. The five YOLO generations from YOLOv8n to YOLO12n ended between 71.4% and 73.9% mAP@0.5, a spread of only 2.5 points. YOLO26n was best on every accuracy metric at 74.8% mAP@0.5 and 35.5% mAP@0.5:0.95, with the highest precision (82.3%), and it needed the least computation of all models at 5.3 GFLOPs. RT-DETR-L, a transformer with about 32 million parameters, was last at 67.5% and ran at 12.2 FPS against 25 to 31 FPS for the YOLO models. On this evidence YOLO26n was chosen as the base of GV-YOLO26.
ablation_para_1: Table 5.3 shows the ablation study, in which the architectural changes were added to YOLO26n one at a time across six genuine design stages; every row was trained on the same SBP-YOLO data under the same schedule and scored once on the leakage-free held-out set. The cost columns behave as designed. Adding the P2 level raises the computation from 5.3 to 6.6 GFLOPs; the LGDH brings it to 6.2, GhostConv to 5.8 and VoVGSCSPC to 5.1 GFLOPs, below YOLO26n, while the parameter count falls from 2.38 to 1.57 million (34% fewer). The accuracy columns do not show an overall gain. YOLO26n reached 81.0% mAP@0.5 and 48.6% mAP@0.5:0.95; going down the ladder, the P2 level changed mAP@0.5:0.95 by −1.0 points; the LGDH changed mAP@0.5:0.95 by −1.1 points; GhostConv changed mAP@0.5:0.95 by +0.8 points; VoVGSCSPC changed mAP@0.5:0.95 by −2.1 points; the NWD loss changed mAP@0.5:0.95 by +0.6 points. The final GV-YOLO26 reached 77.5% mAP@0.5 and 45.8% mAP@0.5:0.95, that is −3.5 and −2.8 points relative to YOLO26n, and the most accurate row was YOLO26n baseline. In PyTorch on the T4 every row ran at a similar single-image speed (55.7 to 59.2 FPS), because at batch size 1 the time is dominated by per-layer overhead and memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic FLOPs.
ablation_para_2: Table 5.4 splits the held-out results by class and adds the scores on the raw test split and on the validation split. For potholes, the small and clustered class that the P2 level and the NWD loss were meant to help, AP@0.5 fell from 72.4% to 71.9% between YOLO26n and GV-YOLO26, and AP@0.5:0.95 fell from 43.6% to 42.5%. For speed bumps, AP@0.5 fell from 89.7% to 83.2%. The raw test split scores every model higher than the held-out set, by 1.4 to 3.6 points of mAP@0.5:0.95, which is the inflation expected from the near-duplicates described in Section 4.8.
ablation_para_3: Two conclusions follow. First, the lightweight modules do their job on cost: the network that predicts on four levels, including a 160 × 160 grid, is smaller and cheaper than YOLO26n. Second, on this dataset the small-object changes did not convert into accuracy. The label statistics explain why. Speed bumps are not small here: the median bump box spans 72% of the image width and only 0% of bumps are smaller than 32 × 32 pixels at 640 × 640, so the stride-4 level has little to add for them. Potholes are the small class (46% of training potholes are under 32 pixels), yet their accuracy did not improve either. A likely reason is that the cheaper convolutions reduce the capacity of the deeper levels that detect most objects, which offsets what the P2 level adds. Differences of about one point between neighbouring stages are within what a single training seed can vary; the gap between YOLO26n and the final model is consistent across the held-out set, the raw test split and the validation split.
distill_note: Note: Val is the 10% validation split used for checkpoint selection; held-out is the leakage-free set. Both distilled models share the architecture and cost of GV-YOLO26. Each row is the best checkpoint on the validation split: epoch 2 of 32 for the run from scratch and epoch 1 of 31 for the fine-tune, both stopped early.
distill_para: Table 5.5 shows the distillation experiments. The teacher is GV-YOLO26 at S scale; on the held-out set it reached 77.7% mAP@0.5 and 47.0% mAP@0.5:0.95, no better than YOLO26n, so it had limited extra knowledge to pass on. Both distillation runs failed. Distilling from scratch with the schedule of Table 4.6 followed the normal run for three epochs and then diverged as the learning-rate warm-up peaked: the classification loss rose from about 3 to above 10 and the validation loss became undefined. Distilling as a low-learning-rate fine-tune of the converged stage-6 model degraded it instead of improving it: validation mAP@0.5:0.95 fell from 47.1% to 25.5% within the first epoch and kept falling, while the distillation loss became negative and reached -1260. A distillation loss cannot be negative if it is correct, so we inspected the box term of BCKD. YOLO26 predicts box distances without DFL and without a positivity constraint; on real images about 0.9% of the student's raw box predictions decode to boxes with negative width or height, and the GIoU between student and teacher boxes then ranged from -10 to 1 instead of lying in [−1, 1]. The term 1 − GIoU is therefore unbounded below, and gradient descent drove it towards minus infinity at the expense of detection. Distillation as implemented here is therefore an honest negative result; clamping the decoded boxes, or distilling only on anchors with valid boxes, is the proposed fix for future investigation.
latency_para: Table 5.3 summarizes the computational complexity, parameter count, and PyTorch FP32 inference throughput of each design stage on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU at batch size 1. Both YOLO26n and GV-YOLO26 operate end-to-end with one-to-one prediction (nms=False), generating final bounding boxes without an external NMS post-processing bottleneck. GV-YOLO26 achieves an end-to-end throughput of 57.5 FPS (17.38 ms per image), closely matching baseline YOLO26n at 58.0 FPS (17.25 ms per image), well above the 24 to 30 FPS requirement for vehicular road preview. While GV-YOLO26 reduces parameter count by 34% (1.57M vs 2.38M) and cuts FLOPs to 5.1 GFLOPs, latency at batch size 1 is primarily bounded by GPU kernel launch overhead and the increased memory traffic of the high-resolution 160 × 160 P2 feature map rather than raw arithmetic FLOPs. The model checkpoint file size is reduced from 5.1 MB to 3.7 MB. Dedicated hardware acceleration via TensorRT engine compilation and embedded deployment on NVIDIA Jetson hardware are analyzed in Section 6.2 as future work.
qual_para_1: Fig. 4.8 and Fig. 4.9 show detections of the final model on held-out road photographs and dashcam frames. The distant bump in Fig. 4.8(a), the kind of target that the baselines found hard in Fig. 5.3, is detected, and in Fig. 4.9 the distant pothole is found while the manhole cover in (a) is also reported as a pothole at low confidence, a typical false positive. Running the same model at a larger input size changes held-out mAP@0.5:0.95 from 45.8% at 640 pixels to 43.3% at 800 and 39.0% at 960, at 8.1 and 11.7 GFLOPs and 44 and 43 FPS in PyTorch, providing a flexible resolution-versus-latency trade-off without retraining.
qual_para_2: Table 5.6 summarises the in-video demo on the four test clips, which cover daytime, rain, dusk and night scenes. Across the clips, 44 distinct tracks crossed the 0.35 confidence threshold in at least one frame, and 26 of them survived temporal confirmation; the other 18 were short-lived detections that would have flashed a warning without a stable hazard behind them. The painted bumps of clips v1 and v2 were confirmed and boxed over consecutive frames as the vehicle approached, including the night scene of v2 (Fig. 4.10).
qual_para_3: The demo also shows the model's weak case. The faded yellow bump in the dusk clip v4 scored at most about 0.36 at 640 pixels and was never confirmed, while dark asphalt patches in the same clip were reported as potholes. Low-contrast markings at dusk are under-represented in the training data, and this is where more data, or a larger input size for distant targets, would help most. Processing ran at 4.9 to 5.1 FPS on the laptop CPU including decoding, tracking and drawing; on the T4 the model alone runs at 57.5 FPS in PyTorch FP32.
video_note: Note: Hazard frames contain at least one confirmed hazard. Raw tracks are distinct ByteTrack tracks that scored at least 0.35 in some frame; confirmed tracks were also seen in three or more frames (equation 4.7). FPS is end-to-end processing speed (decoding, inference, tracking, drawing) on the laptop CPU.
cmp_para: Three things distinguish GV-YOLO26 in this comparison. It covers both speed bumps and potholes, the two anomalies a suspension controller must react to. It is the only model in the table built on an end-to-end detector, so its inference pipeline has no NMS stage. And it is evaluated on images that share no source photo or video with its training data, against a YOLO26n trained under the same protocol; several of the higher figures in the literature come from private datasets whose splits cannot be checked for the kind of leakage documented in Section 4.8.
disc_base: In our benchmark YOLO26n led every accuracy metric and needed the least computation. Its end-to-end head also suits the vehicle setting: removing NMS makes latency independent of the number of detections and removes a threshold that would otherwise have to be tuned on the road. The ablation confirms it as a strong starting point: no design stage beat it on the held-out set.
disc_gain: The cheap modules paid for the P2 level as intended: the final model has 34% fewer parameters and 4% less computation than YOLO26n. The accuracy expectation did not hold on this dataset: neither the P2 level nor the NWD loss improved held-out accuracy, and the final model is −3.5 points of mAP@0.5 from YOLO26n. GV-YOLO26, as built here, is an efficiency-oriented variant of YOLO26n rather than a more accurate one.
disc_cost: A cost that FLOP counts hide.

A high-resolution P2 map increases memory traffic and layer invocation overhead more than arithmetic, so a model with fewer FLOPs does not necessarily run faster at batch size 1. In PyTorch on the T4 every row ran at a similar single-image speed (55.7 to 59.2 FPS), because at batch size 1 the time is dominated by per-layer overhead and memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic FLOPs. In PyTorch FP32 on the Tesla T4, GV-YOLO26 ran at 57.5 FPS, comfortably satisfying the 24 to 30 frames per second requirement for real-time vehicular control.
disc_baselines: Moving from YOLOv8n to YOLO12n changed mAP@0.5 by only 2.5 points on the test split. A newer generation alone adds little on this task, and the ablation shows that the architectural changes tried here did not add accuracy either; the clearest lever left is the data, in particular more low-contrast, dusk and night-time bumps.
disc_limits_prev: Relation to the limitations identified earlier.

GV-YOLO26 keeps its cost below that of its base model, runs without NMS, and is evaluated on public data under a repeatable, leakage-free protocol, which addresses the deployment and reproducibility limitations listed in Section 3.2. The small-object limitation is only partly addressed: the extra P2 level is affordable, but on this dataset it did not raise accuracy.
disc_limits: Every model was trained once with one seed (seed 42), so differences of about one point between neighbouring stages should not be over-read. The raw SBP-YOLO dataset contains augmented copies of the same photos across its folders; the held-out set removes them, but at 482 images it is smaller than the raw test split. The distillation experiments were limited by the loss defect described in Section 5.4.3. Latency was measured in PyTorch on a cloud T4 GPU rather than on an embedded automotive board, and the video demo uses four short dashcam-style clips rather than a continuous road test.
ch5_summary: Among seven stock detectors trained under one protocol on the SBP-YOLO dataset, YOLO26n was the most accurate and the cheapest, and it was chosen as the base of GV-YOLO26. With a P2 level, the LGDH, GhostConv and VoVGSCSPC, GV-YOLO26 needs 1.57 million parameters and 5.1 GFLOPs, 34% fewer parameters than YOLO26n. On a leakage-free held-out set it reached 77.5% mAP@0.5 against 81.0% for YOLO26n trained identically, trading a few points of accuracy for a smaller model. In PyTorch FP32 the final model runs at 57.5 FPS on a Tesla T4, distillation did not help due to an unbounded box-loss issue, and the video demo confirms hazards across frames to suppress short-lived false alarms.
ch6_summary_2: We first benchmarked seven stock detectors on the SBP-YOLO dataset under a single fixed protocol and selected YOLO26n, the most accurate and cheapest of them, as the base. On it we designed GV-YOLO26, which rebuilds the backbone and neck with GhostConv and VoVGSCSPC, adds a P2 detection level with a lightweight grouped head, and trains with an NWD-augmented loss and weather augmentation; distillation from a larger teacher was tested. We trained every design stage through an ablation ladder on the SBP-YOLO dataset, audited and removed train–test leakage before evaluating, profiled computational latency, and built an in-video demo that tracks hazards across frames and warns only about confirmed ones.
outcomes: In a measured benchmark of seven stock detectors on the SBP-YOLO dataset, YOLO generations from YOLOv8n to YOLO12n differed by only 2.5 points of mAP@0.5, and YOLO26n was best at 74.8% with the lowest cost of 5.3 GFLOPs.

GV-YOLO26 was built on YOLO26n with a GhostConv–VoVGSCSPC backbone and neck, a P2 detection level and a Lightweight Grouped Detection Head; it has 1.57 million parameters and 5.1 GFLOPs, against 2.38 million and 5.3 GFLOPs for YOLO26n (34% fewer parameters).

Train–test leakage was audited in the SBP-YOLO dataset (526 of 1,125 test images share a source photo with training images) and a 482-image leakage-free held-out set was established for all primary evaluations.
On that set GV-YOLO26 reached 77.5% mAP@0.5 and 45.8% mAP@0.5:0.95, against 81.0% and 48.6% for YOLO26n: achieving a significantly smaller model at a small cost in accuracy.
Knowledge distillation did not help; the cause was traced to an unbounded box-distillation term on invalid student box predictions, which is documented with evidence and a proposed fix.
End-to-end PyTorch FP32 inference throughput was measured at 57.5 FPS (17.38 ms) on a Tesla T4 GPU, with final detections and no separate NMS post-processing step.
An in-video demo with ByteTrack and three-frame confirmation reduced 44 raw hazard tracks to 26 confirmed ones on four test clips, eliminating short-lived false alarms.
The complete pipeline is built on the open Ultralytics framework and public data, ensuring full reproducibility on standard GPU environments.
objectives_met: Chapter 2 reviewed over 40 sources and identified four key research gaps in road hazard detection
Seven stock detectors trained and evaluated on the SBP-YOLO dataset; YOLO26n selected as optimal base
GhostConv, VoVGSCSPC, P2 level and LGDH integrated; one configuration per design stage; 34% fewer parameters than YOLO26n
All six ablation stages, the teacher and two distillation runs trained and scored on a leakage-free held-out set (Tables 5.3 to 5.5); distillation failure diagnosed
Inference latency profiled in PyTorch FP32 on Tesla T4 (57.5 FPS, 17.38 ms); TensorRT export and embedded Jetson deployment formulated as future scope
objectives_met_video: demo_video.py with ByteTrack and three-frame confirmation; 44 raw tracks reduced to 26 confirmed hazards on four clips (Table 5.6)
conclusion_1: GV-YOLO26 shows that the extra high-resolution detection level that small targets call for can be paid for with cheaper convolutions and a lighter head: the final model predicts on four levels, including a 160 × 160 grid, yet is 33.7% smaller than the YOLO26n it was built from, and runs end-to-end without NMS. On the accuracy side the result is honest: on images that share nothing with the training data, the design did not beat an identically trained YOLO26n; it traded a few points of mAP for a substantially smaller model. Finding and removing train–test leakage was one of the most important contributions of the project, because without it every model would have appeared artificially inflated by several points.
conclusion_2: The work also clarified what is still needed before such a detector can be integrated into an active vehicle suspension system. Its accuracy on faint, low-contrast bumps at dusk and night must improve through targeted data collection, and hardware acceleration via TensorRT on an embedded board such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier remains the natural deployment path. These directions form the future scope of this work.
future_seed: repeat every training run with several seeds to report the mean and spread of each result; the differences between neighbouring design stages are small enough that a single seed cannot always separate them from run-to-run variation.
future_trt: compile and benchmark the model into TensorRT FP16 and INT8 engines on dedicated automotive edge hardware such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier or Jetson Orin Nano. While preliminary TensorRT FP16 conversion on a server GPU indicated potential speeds exceeding 100 FPS, naive INT8 post-training quantization degraded accuracy to 35.0% mAP@0.5:0.95; future work must employ Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) to preserve detection quality at 8-bit precision.
sdg_map: Under Target 3.6, the focus of GV-YOLO26 on small, distant targets matters because the bump that is seen late is the one that causes injury, and the temporal confirmation of the video demo keeps false warnings, which drivers learn to ignore, rare. Under Targets 9.1 and 9.5, the project contributes a documented design, a repeatable baseline benchmark and a leakage-free evaluation protocol. Under Target 11.2, the small size of the model, 1.57 million parameters and 5.1 GFLOPs, keeps the computational overhead low enough for wide adoption in intelligent transportation systems.
